intro: In December 1891, a class of eighteen men in Springfield, Massachusetts, was stuck indoors for the winter. Their teacher, James Naismith, nailed two peach baskets to a balcony railing. He handed them a soccer ball and thirteen typed rules. Basketball began in that one small gym.

In this unit you will follow the game out of that room. YMCA graduates carried it to other cities and countries. Colleges formed teams, and Senda Berenson wrote rules for women at Smith College. Illinois high schools held state tournaments, first for boys in 1908 and for girls in 1977.

You will be able to explain why the goal is ten feet high and why backboards appeared. You will name the people, places and dates that shaped the game. You will also tell who was left out of some tournaments, and which law helped open the door.
bigQuestion: How did the room where basketball began shape the game, and how did new rooms and new rule books change who could play?

test.q: Why did Naismith need a new game in December 1891?
choices: his class was stuck indoors for winter
test.why: Winter kept the Springfield class indoors, and the old games were too rough.

test.q: Who asked Naismith to invent an indoor game?
test.why: Luther Gulick led physical education at the school.

test.q: What ball did the first game use?
test.why: No basketball existed yet, so the class used a soccer ball.

test.q: Why is the goal ten feet high?
choices: the Springfield balcony railing was about that high
test.why: The baskets were nailed to a railing about ten feet up.

test.q: How many rules did Naismith first post?
test.why: He typed thirteen rules for the bulletin board.

choices: to block fans on the balcony
test.why: Balcony fans could reach the ball, so a board shielded it.

test.q: How did the ancient Maya ballcourt relate to basketball?
choices: it was a much older, separate game
test.why: The Mesoamerican game is ancient, but basketball was invented new in 1891.

test.q: How did the game reach other cities so quickly?
test.why: Graduates of the Springfield school took it to the YMCAs they led.

choices: an early intercollegiate game, won 9–3 over Hamline
test.why: The Minnesota State School of Agriculture beat Hamline 9–3.

test.q: What did Senda Berenson's rules do?
test.why: Her rules divided the court into three zones.

test.q: In which year did the IHSA crown its first boys basketball champion?
test.why: The first boys state tournament was held in 1908.

test.q: Which law, passed in 1972, helped open school sports to girls?
test.why: Title IX bans sex discrimination in federally funded school programs.

test.q: In which year did the IHSA crown its first girls basketball champion?
test.why: The first IHSA girls champion came in 1977, five years after Title IX.

test.q: Where was the first Olympic basketball final played?
test.why: The 1936 final was played outdoors in Berlin.

write.prompt: Did the room where basketball began matter more than the rules that were written later? Use at least two dates and documents from this unit, such as Naismith's thirteen rules printed in The Triangle (1892), Berenson's women's rules (1901), IHSA tournament records (1908 and 1977) or Title IX (1972). Explain what each one shows about who could play and how the game took its shape.
tips: Name each document or record and give its year.
Tell what the Springfield gym added, like the ten-foot height or the backboard.
Compare a rule from one book with a rule from another.
Say who could take part at each date, and what changed it.
